claim: Inflammatory caspases are cysteine protease zymogens whose activation following infection or cellular damage occurs within supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs) known as inflammasomes.
source: Inflammatory caspases are cysteine protease zymogens whose activation following infection or cellular damage occurs within supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs) known as inflammasomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about inflammatory caspases and inflammasomes.

claim: Inflammasomes recruit caspases to undergo proximity-induced autoprocessing into an enzymatically active form that cleaves downstream targets.
source: Inflammasomes recruit caspases to undergo proximity-induced autoprocessing into an enzymatically active form that cleaves downstream targets.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of caspase activation within inflammasomes.

claim: Binding of bacterial LPS to its cytosolic sensor, caspase-11 (Casp11), promotes Casp11 aggregation within a high-molecular-weight complex known as the noncanonical inflammasome.
source: Binding of bacterial LPS to its cytosolic sensor, caspase-11 (Casp11), promotes Casp11 aggregation within a high-molecular-weight complex known as the noncanonical inflammasome, where it is activated to cleave gasdermin D and induce pyroptosis.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the noncanonical inflammasome pathway.

claim: Activated Casp11 cleaves gasdermin D and induces pyroptosis.
source: Binding of bacterial LPS to its cytosolic sensor, caspase-11 (Casp11), promotes Casp11 aggregation within a high-molecular-weight complex known as the noncanonical inflammasome, where it is activated to cleave gasdermin D and induce pyroptosis.
evidence: This describes the established downstream effects of Casp11 activation.

claim: The cellular correlates of Casp11 oligomerization and whether Casp11 forms an LPS-induced SMOC within cells remain unknown.
source: However, the cellular correlates of Casp11 oligomerization and whether Casp11 forms an LPS-induced SMOC within cells remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Expression of fluorescently labeled Casp11 in macrophages revealed that cytosolic LPS induced Casp11 speck formation.
source: Expression of fluorescently labeled Casp11 in macrophages revealed that cytosolic LPS induced Casp11 speck formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E demonstrating LPS-induced speck formation.

claim: Catalytic activity and autoprocessing were required for Casp11 to form LPS-induced specks in macrophages.
source: Unexpectedly, catalytic activity and autoprocessing were required for Casp11 to form LPS-induced specks in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and 1E showing that C254A and D285A mutants fail to form specks.

claim: Both catalytic activity and autoprocessing were required for Casp11 speck formation in an ectopic expression system.
source: Furthermore, both catalytic activity and autoprocessing were required for Casp11 speck formation in an ectopic expression system, and processing of Casp11 via ectopically expressed TEV protease was sufficient to induce Casp11 speck formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and 2C showing speck formation requirements in HEK293T cells.

claim: Processing of Casp11 via ectopically expressed TEV protease was sufficient to induce Casp11 speck formation.
source: Furthermore, both catalytic activity and autoprocessing were required for Casp11 speck formation in an ectopic expression system, and processing of Casp11 via ectopically expressed TEV protease was sufficient to induce Casp11 speck formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7C and 7D showing TEV-induced speck formation.

claim: The mammalian innate immune system relies on evolutionarily conserved pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
source: The mammalian innate immune system relies on evolutionarily conserved pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) in order to rapidly respond to potential microbial threats (Blander and Sander, 2012; Janeway, 1989; Janeway and Medzhitov, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A common feature of PRR activation is their inducible assembly into higher-order oligomeric protein complexes, termed supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs).
source: A common feature of PRR activation is their inducible assembly into higher-order oligomeric protein complexes, termed supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs), which mediate the effector function of the PRR signaling pathway in response to microbial infection or pathologic stimulus (Kagan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Caspases-1 and -11 are inflammatory caspases that are recruited into inflammasome SMOCs in response to the cytosolic presence of pathogen-derived signals or molecules.
source: Caspases-1 and -11 are inflammatory caspases that are recruited into inflammasome SMOCs in response to the cytosolic presence of pathogen-derived signals or molecules (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inflammatory caspases are zymogens that contain a C-terminal enzymatic domain and an N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD).
source: Inflammatory caspases are zymogens that contain a C-terminal enzymatic domain and an N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), which promotes SMOC formation through homotypic interactions with other CARD-containing adapter proteins as well as homodimerization with each other (Lu et al., 2014; Park et al., 2007; Ting and Davis, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature describing caspase structure.

claim: The CARD promotes SMOC formation through homotypic interactions with other CARD-containing adapter proteins as well as homodimerization.
source: Inflammatory caspases are zymogens that contain a C-terminal enzymatic domain and an N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), which promotes SMOC formation through homotypic interactions with other CARD-containing adapter proteins as well as homodimerization with each other (Lu et al., 2014; Park et al., 2007; Ting and Davis, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The C-terminal enzymatic domain of caspases is comprised of large (17–20 kDa) and small (10–12 kDa) subunits separated by an interdomain linker (IDL).
source: The C-terminal enzymatic domain of caspases is comprised of large (17–20 kDa) and small (10–12 kDa) subunits separated by an interdomain linker (IDL), which contains the self-cleavage site that undergoes autoprocessing following caspase oligomerization (Ross et al., 2022; Walker et al., 1994; Wilson et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature describing caspase structure.

claim: The interdomain linker (IDL) contains the self-cleavage site that undergoes autoprocessing following caspase oligomerization.
source: The C-terminal enzymatic domain of caspases is comprised of large (17–20 kDa) and small (10–12 kDa) subunits separated by an interdomain linker (IDL), which contains the self-cleavage site that undergoes autoprocessing following caspase oligomerization (Ross et al., 2022; Walker et al., 1994; Wilson et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Caspase-1 is recruited to canonical inflammasome complexes that typically contain a sensor protein of the NLR family, the adaptor protein ASC, and caspase-1 itself.
source: Caspase-1 is recruited to canonical inflammasome complexes that typically contain a sensor protein of the NLR family, the adaptor protein ASC, and caspase-1 itself (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Caspase-11 (Casp11) binds directly to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria.
source: In contrast, caspase-11 (Casp11) binds directly to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria (Shi et al., 2014) and does not require a known sensor or adapter for activation of pyroptosis via a pathway termed the noncanonical inflammasome (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Casp11 does not require a known sensor or adapter for activation of pyroptosis via the noncanonical inflammasome pathway.
source: In contrast, caspase-11 (Casp11) binds directly to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria (Shi et al., 2014) and does not require a known sensor or adapter for activation of pyroptosis via a pathway termed the noncanonical inflammasome (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Recruitment of Casp1 and Casp11 to their respective SMOCs results in their autoprocessing, a process termed proximity-induced activation.
source: Recruitment of Casp1 and Casp11 to their respective SMOCs results in their autoprocessing, a process termed proximity-induced activation, enabling their cleavage of downstream targets (Salvesen and Dixit, 1999; Shi, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp11-dependent cleavage of gasdermin D (GSDMD) leads to cell lysis and release of inflammatory cellular contents, triggering pyroptosis.
source: Casp11-dependent cleavage of its target, gasdermin D (GSDMD), leads to cell lysis, as well as release of inflammatory cellular contents, thus triggering pyroptosis, a pro-inflammatory programmed cell death (Aglietti et al., 2016; Kayagaki et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp1 and Casp11 play important roles in antimicrobial host defense.
source: As a result, Casp1 and Casp11 play important roles in antimicrobial host defense, but they can also promote autoinflammatory disease when dysregulated (Franchi et al., 2009; Hagar et al., 2013; Henao-Mejia et al., 2012; Kayagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp1 and Casp11 can promote autoinflammatory disease when dysregulated.
source: As a result, Casp1 and Casp11 play important roles in antimicrobial host defense, but they can also promote autoinflammatory disease when dysregulated (Franchi et al., 2009; Hagar et al., 2013; Henao-Mejia et al., 2012; Kayagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inducible dimerization is used to model assembly of functional caspase complexes within cells.
source: Inducible dimerization is used to model assembly of functional caspase complexes within cells (Ball et al., 2020; Boucher et al., 2018; Oberst et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp11 mutants whose autoprocessing site is ablated have significantly reduced protease activity toward their substrates despite being dimerized and having an intact catalytic site.
source: Interestingly, Casp11 mutants, whose autoprocessing site is ablated, have significantly reduced protease activity toward their substrates and have defective ability to induce cell death, despite being dimerized and having an intact catalytic site (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CRISPR targeting of Casp11 autoprocessing or catalytic activity demonstrates that both are important for Casp11-dependent pyroptosis and lethal sepsis.
source: Furthermore, CRISPR targeting of Casp11 autoprocessing or catalytic activity demonstrates that both are important for Casp11-dependent pyroptosis and lethal sepsis (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-cleavable Casp8 is active in vitro or in the presence of kosmotropic salts.
source: Interestingly, while non-cleavable Casp8 is active in vitro (Chang et al., 2003) or in the presence of kosmotropic salts (Pop et al., 2007), autoprocessing is also required for full Casp8 activity toward its substrates within cells, implying that autoprocessing stabilizes the active form of the enzyme (Oberst et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Autoprocessing is required for full Casp8 activity toward its substrates within cells.
source: Interestingly, while non-cleavable Casp8 is active in vitro (Chang et al., 2003) or in the presence of kosmotropic salts (Pop et al., 2007), autoprocessing is also required for full Casp8 activity toward its substrates within cells, implying that autoprocessing stabilizes the active form of the enzyme (Oberst et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Autoprocessing stabilizes the active form of Casp8.
source: Interestingly, while non-cleavable Casp8 is active in vitro (Chang et al., 2003) or in the presence of kosmotropic salts (Pop et al., 2007), autoprocessing is also required for full Casp8 activity toward its substrates within cells, implying that autoprocessing stabilizes the active form of the enzyme (Oberst et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited literature.

claim: Casp1 requires autoprocessing for robust cleavage of IL-1β.
source: This parallels recent findings with Casp1, which requires autoprocessing for robust cleavage of IL-1β (Broz et al., 2010) and GSDMD (Ball et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp1 requires autoprocessing for robust cleavage of GSDMD.
source: This parallels recent findings with Casp1, which requires autoprocessing for robust cleavage of IL-1β (Broz et al., 2010) and GSDMD (Ball et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ASC fluorescent reporters have enabled the dynamic tracking of canonical inflammasome assembly within cells.
source: However, while ASC fluorescent reporters have enabled the dynamic tracking of canonical inflammasome assembly within cells (Stutz et al., 2013; Tzeng et al., 2016), the cellular correlates of Casp11 oligomerization within cells in response to cytosolic LPS remain poorly defined.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp11WT-mCherry, but not Casp11C254A-mCherry, restored GSDMD cleavage and pore formation in Casp11-/- BMDMs.
source: Casp11WT-mCherry, but not Casp11C254A-mCherry, restored GSDMD cleavage and pore formation in Casp11-/- BMDMs, indicating that the tagged Casp11-mCherry construct retains functionality (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Casp11D285A-mCherry expression failed to completely ablate pore formation despite abrogating GSDMD cleavage.
source: Interestingly, Casp11D285A-mCherry expression failed to completely ablate pore formation despite abrogating GSDMD cleavage, indicating that tagged Casp11-mCherry carries out GSDMD cleavage in a manner dependent on its autoprocessing (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Casp11-/- BMDMs transduced with Casp11WT-mCherry, Casp11C254A-mCherry, or Casp11D285A-mCherry exhibited diffuse cytoplasmic staining in the absence of LPS stimulation.
source: As expected, Casp11-/- BMDMs transduced with Casp11WT-mCherry, Casp11C254A-mCherry, or Casp11D285A-mCherry exhibited diffuse cytoplasmic staining in the absence of LPS stimulation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Casp11WT-mCherry coalesced into large specks in response to transfection of LPS.
source: Notably, Casp11WT-mCherry coalesced into large specks in response to transfection of LPS, consistent with the concept that Casp11 assembles into an LPS-induced higher-order complex, or SMOC (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Casp11C254A-mCherry and Casp11D285A-mCherry-transduced cells were unable to form specks in response to LPS.
source: In contrast, Casp11C254A-mCherry and Casp11D285A-mCherry-transduced cells were unable to form specks in response to LPS (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: CARD-dependent binding of Casp11 to LPS is not sufficient to mediate Casp11 speck formation within cells.
source: These findings imply that CARD-dependent binding of Casp11 to LPS is not sufficient to mediate Casp11 speck formation within cells, and that Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing facilitate higher order assembly of noncanonical inflammasomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that catalytic activity and autoprocessing are required for speck formation.

claim: Cells expressing Casp11WT-mCherry exhibited speck formation upon infection with L. pneumophila.
source: Notably, cells expressing Casp11WT-mCherry exhibited speck formation upon infection with L. pneumophila, similarly to cells exposed to transfected LPS alone (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: L. pneumophila infection induced speck formation in cells expressing Casp11C254A-mCherry, in contrast to findings with cytosolic LPS.
source: Interestingly, L. pneumophila infection also induced speck formation in cells expressing Casp11C254A-mCherry, in contrast to our findings with cytosolic LPS (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: In addition to LPS itself, other properties associated with intact bacteria promote Casp11 oligomerization and inflammasome activation.
source: These data suggest that in addition to LPS itself, other properties associated with intact bacteria promote Casp11 oligomerization and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that bacterial infection induces speck formation in catalytically inactive Casp11.

claim: Co-expression of Casp11WT-mCherry and GSDMD led to dose-dependent GSDMD cleavage and cell death that required Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing.
source: Consistent with previous observations, co-expression of Casp11WT-mCherry and GSDMD led to dose-dependent GSDMD cleavage and cell death that required Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Lee et al., 2018; Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, as well as citations to prior literature.

claim: Casp11WT-mCherry spontaneously assembled into large aggregates in HEK293T cells.
source: Notably, Casp11WT-mCherry spontaneously assembled into large aggregates reminiscent of ASC-containing specks (Stutz et al., 2013; Tzeng et al., 2016), whereas Casp11C254A-mCherry and Casp11D285A-mCherry remained diffuse throughout the cytosol, consistent with our previous finding in macrophages that Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing are necessary to initiate or propagate Casp11 inflammasome assembly (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Casp11C254A-mCherry and Casp11D285A-mCherry remained diffuse throughout the cytosol in HEK293T cells.
source: Notably, Casp11WT-mCherry spontaneously assembled into large aggregates reminiscent of ASC-containing specks (Stutz et al., 2013; Tzeng et al., 2016), whereas Casp11C254A-mCherry and Casp11D285A-mCherry remained diffuse throughout the cytosol, consistent with our previous finding in macrophages that Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing are necessary to initiate or propagate Casp11 inflammasome assembly (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK (zVAD) blocked spontaneous speck assembly and autoprocessing by Casp11WT-mCherry in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, the pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK (zVAD) blocked spontaneous speck assembly and autoprocessing by Casp11WT-mCherry in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Casp11C254A-mCherry did not aggregate into visible specks, and its cytoplasmic distribution was not detectably altered in the presence of zVAD.
source: Consistently, Casp11C254A-mCherry did not aggregate into visible specks, and its cytoplasmic distribution was not detectably altered in the presence of zVAD.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Similar doses of zVAD abrogated LPS-induced Casp11-mediated pyroptosis in BMDMs.
source: Similar doses of zVAD abrogated LPS-induced Casp11-mediated pyroptosis in BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Catalytic activity was not required for Casp11 self-association.
source: Importantly, and consistent with prior studies (Shi et al., 2014), catalytic activity was not required for Casp11 self-association per se, as Casp11WT and Casp11C254A associate both with themselves and each other in reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Casp11WT and Casp11C254A associate both with themselves and each other in reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations.
source: Importantly, and consistent with prior studies (Shi et al., 2014), catalytic activity was not required for Casp11 self-association per se, as Casp11WT and Casp11C254A associate both with themselves and each other in reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Catalytic activity plays an important role in higher-order Casp11 oligomerization in response to cytosolic LPS.
source: Together, these data imply that catalytic activity plays an important role in higher-order Casp11 oligomerization in response to cytosolic LPS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that catalytic activity is required for speck formation but not for self-association.

claim: LPS transfection induced speck formation in 2xFLAG-Casp11WT-expressing cells, but not in 2xFLAG-Casp11C254A cells.
source: Importantly, LPS transfection induced speck formation in 2xFLAG-Casp11WT-expressing cells, but not in 2xFLAG-Casp11C254A cells, consistent with our findings in BMDMs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhibition of catalytic activity with the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD blocked formation of specks in 2xFLAG-Casp11WT-expressing cells.
source: Moreover, inhibition of catalytic activity with the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD also blocked formation of specks in 2xFLAG-Casp11WT-expressing cells, consistent with our previous findings (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Both the N- and C-terminal portions of Casp11 were found within specks by microscopy.
source: Our finding that both N- and C-terminal portions of Casp11 were found within specks by microscopy, despite evidence that Casp11 processing was taking place, suggested that both the N- and C-terminal domains of Casp11 were simultaneously present within the same large specks.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: Casp11WT-mCherry induced spontaneous formation of specks in HEK293T cells stably expressing 2xFLAG-Casp11WT, which recruited WT 2xFLAG-Casp11.
source: Notably, Casp11WT-mCherry induced spontaneous formation of specks, which recruited WT 2xFLAG-Casp11, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Casp11-mCherry specks recruited catalytically inactive 2xFLAG-Casp11C254A.
source: Critically, Casp11-mCherry specks also recruited catalytically inactive 2xFLAG-Casp11C254A, demonstrating that both N- and C-termini are present within the specks and that catalytically inactive Casp11 can be recruited to complexes formed by the wild-type protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Catalytically inactive Casp11 can be recruited to complexes formed by the wild-type protein.
source: Critically, Casp11-mCherry specks also recruited catalytically inactive 2xFLAG-Casp11C254A, demonstrating that both N- and C-termini are present within the specks and that catalytically inactive Casp11 can be recruited to complexes formed by the wild-type protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing levels of unlabeled Casp11 significantly increased speck formation by Casp11C254A-mCherry.
source: In contrast, and consistent with our observations in stable 2xFLAG-Casp11C254A-expressing cells, co-transfection of unlabeled Casp11 significantly increased speck formation by Casp11C254A-mCherry (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: WT Casp11 rescues oligomerization of catalytically inactive Casp11-mCherry species by enabling recruitment of the mutant protein to WT complexes.
source: These findings demonstrate that WT Casp11 rescues oligomerization of catalytically inactive Casp11-mCherry species by enabling recruitment of the mutant protein to WT complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that WT Casp11 can induce speck formation in catalytically inactive mutants.

claim: Mutating the IDL autoprocessing site of Casp11C254A-mCherry to yield Casp11C254A/D285A-mCherry prevented IDL processing but did not prevent formation of mCherry specks in the presence of unlabeled WT Casp11.
source: Intriguingly, mutating the IDL autoprocessing site of Casp11C254A-mCherry to yield an inactive, IDL-uncleavable mutant Casp11C254A/D285A-mCherry prevented IDL processing but did not prevent formation of mCherry specks in the presence of unlabeled WT Casp11 (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: Neither co-transfected Casp11C254A-mCherry nor Casp11C254A/D285A-mCherry impaired pyroptosis or GSDMD cleavage by WT Casp11.
source: Importantly, neither co-transfected Casp11C254A-mCherry nor Casp11C254A/D285A-mCherry impaired pyroptosis or GSDMD cleavage by WT Casp11 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Catalytic activity and autoprocessing are required for the formation of higher-order oligomeric Casp11 complexes.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that catalytic activity and autoprocessing are required for the formation of higher-order oligomeric Casp11 complexes, and that recruitment of inactive Casp11 to these complexes is independent of IDL trans-processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Recruitment of inactive Casp11 to higher-order complexes is independent of IDL trans-processing.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that catalytic activity and autoprocessing are required for the formation of higher-order oligomeric Casp11 complexes, and that recruitment of inactive Casp11 to these complexes is independent of IDL trans-processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that non-cleavable mutants can still be recruited to WT complexes.

claim: WT Casp11 could undergo autoprocessing, which required catalytic activity and IDL autoprocessing.
source: As expected, WT Casp11 could undergo autoprocessing, which required catalytic activity and IDL autoprocessing (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: WT Casp11 rescued speck formation by catalytically inactive Casp11C254A-mCherry.
source: Consistent with our prior observations, WT Casp11 rescued speck formation by catalytically inactive Casp11C254A-mCherry (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Neither the catalytic Casp11C254A nor the autoprocessing Casp11D285A mutants could recruit Casp11C254A-mCherry to specks.
source: However, neither the catalytic Casp11C254A nor the autoprocessing Casp11D285A mutants could recruit Casp11C254A-mCherry to specks (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Casp11C254A-mCherry did not impair Casp11-mediated cytotoxicity in HEK293T cells stably expressing GSDMD.
source: Importantly, Casp11C254A-mCherry did not impair Casp11-mediated cytotoxicity in HEK293T cells stably expressing GSDMD, as evidenced by LDH release (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing must be present within the same molecule and occur upstream of Casp11 inflammasome assembly.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate a key role for Casp11 catalytic activity and autoprocessing in assembly of higher-order Casp11 inflammasome complexes. These findings also indicate that these activities must be present within the same molecule and occur upstream of Casp11 inflammasome assembly, rather than occurring downstream of inflammasome assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that mutants lacking catalytic activity or autoprocessing cannot form specks on their own.

claim: DmrB-(ΔCARD)-Casp11-mCherry displayed basal levels of speck formation above background, which was significantly increased by addition of dimerizer.
source: Interestingly, DmrB-(ΔCARD)-Casp11-mCherry displayed basal levels of speck formation above background, which was significantly increased by addition of dimerizer (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Both baseline and dimerization-induced speck formation of DmrB-(ΔCARD)-Casp11-mCherry required catalytic activity.
source: Critically, both baseline and dimerization-induced speck formation of DmrB-(ΔCARD)-Casp11-mCherry required catalytic activity, consistent with our finding that catalytic activity is essential for Casp11 speck formation in response to cytosolic LPS (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: DmrB-(ΔCARD)-Casp11-mCherry-induced GSDMD cleavage required dimerization and catalytic activity.
source: Importantly, DmrB-(ΔCARD)-Casp11-mCherry-induced GSDMD cleavage required dimerization and catalytic activity, indicating that these constructs are functional and consistent with previous observations that dimerization induces catalytic activity of initiator and inflammatory caspases (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, as well as a citation to prior literature.

claim: CARD-less Casp11-mCherry spontaneously assembled into specks in the transient 293T transfection system.
source: Surprisingly, CARD-less Casp11-mCherry spontaneously assembled into specks in the transient 293T transfection system, and this was abrogated by mutation of the catalytic cysteine, further supporting the model that higher-order oligomerization of Casp11 in response to LPS requires its enzymatic activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: A CARD-only-citrine fusion protein was unable to form specks, in contrast to the corresponding full-length Casp11-citrine fusion.
source: Moreover, a CARD-only-citrine fusion protein was unable to form specks, in contrast to the corresponding full-length Casp11-citrine fusion, further demonstrating that the enzymatic domain is vital for Casp11 oligomerization (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Higher-order oligomerization of Casp11 requires the catalytic activity and autoprocessing function of the enzymatic domain.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that higher-order oligomerization of Casp11 requires the catalytic activity and autoprocessing function of the enzymatic domain, and that the CARD is insufficient to mediate SMOC formation in response to cytosolic LPS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that CARD-less constructs can form specks but CARD-only constructs cannot.

claim: The CARD is insufficient to mediate SMOC formation in response to cytosolic LPS.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that higher-order oligomerization of Casp11 requires the catalytic activity and autoprocessing function of the enzymatic domain, and that the CARD is insufficient to mediate SMOC formation in response to cytosolic LPS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that CARD-only constructs cannot form specks.

claim: Co-expression of TEV protease with either WT or C254A Casp11TEV-mCherry in HEK293T cells resulted in dose-dependent cleavage of both constructs.
